title: Kenyan Beef Bone Soup
community: Enjoyed across all Kenyan communities — especially popular at butcheries
author: Mama Wanjiru
desc: Supu ya Mfupa is Kenya's most restorative soup — beef bones simmered for hours with onions, tomatoes, garlic, ginger, and spices until the broth is rich, deeply flavourful, and nourishing. Sold at every Kenyan butchery and known for being the ultimate remedy for a cold or a long day.
longDesc: Supu ya mfupa is the Kenyan version of bone broth — long before it became a global wellness trend, Kenyans were simmering beef bones for hours to extract every drop of nutrition and flavour from them. The result is a rich, golden, deeply savoury broth with soft, succulent meat falling from the bones. At Kenyan butcheries, a cup of supu is often served as a starter before the main meat, and it has a legendary reputation as a cure-all.
ingredients: 1.5 kg beef bones — knuckle, marrow, or neck bones
steps: Roast the bones (optional but recommended): place on a baking tray at 200°C for 20 minutes until lightly browned. This deepens the flavour dramatically.
Place the bones in a large pot. Cover with cold water and bring to a boil. Boil for 5 minutes and discard this first water — it removes impurities.
Add 2 litres of fresh cold water. Add the onions, tomatoes, garlic, ginger, carrots, celery, peppercorns, bay leaves, curry powder, and paprika.
Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat to the lowest setting. Simmer partially covered for 2—3 hours. The broth should bubble gently, never boil aggressively.
Skim any foam or fat from the surface every 30 minutes for the clearest broth.
Season with salt in the final 30 minutes.
Taste and adjust. Serve hot with coriander and a squeeze of lemon, with pieces of the marrow bones for scooping.
chefTips: Roasting the bones first is not strictly necessary but creates a dramatically richer, darker broth.
The first boil-and-discard removes blood and impurities — do not skip it for a clean-tasting soup.
Never boil aggressively — the fat emulsifies into the broth and makes it cloudy and greasy.
Marrow bones are the most prized — scoop the marrow out with a small spoon and eat it spread on chapati.
commonMistakes: Skipping the first boil-and-discard — produces a murky, slightly gamey broth.
Boiling too vigorously — makes the broth cloudy and greasy.
Not simmering long enough — the richness comes from time.

faqs.a: Knuckle bones give the most gelatin; marrow bones give richness; neck bones give meat and flavour. A combination of all three makes the best supu.

faqs.q: Can I use a pressure cooker?
faqs.a: Yes — pressure cook for 45—60 minutes for a similarly rich broth in much less time.

cookingScience: Long simmering of beef bones extracts collagen from the connective tissue and cartilage, converting it into gelatin. This gelatin gives supu its characteristic silky mouthfeel and body. Roasting the bones first creates Maillard compounds on the surface that dissolve into the broth during simmering, creating the rich, complex flavour of a good bone soup.
sustainabilityTips: Bones are among the most underutilised parts of the animal — supu makes full use of them.
Freeze leftover broth in ice cube trays for use as stock in other recipes.
The strained vegetables can be composted.
storage: Refrigerate for up to 4 days — fat solidifies on top and can be removed. Freeze for up to 3 months.
reheating: Reheat gently on the stovetop until hot throughout.
healthBenefits: Rich in collagen and gelatin — supports joint, gut, and skin health.
Provides minerals including calcium, phosphorus, and magnesium from the bones.
Easily digestible — one of the gentlest and most nourishing foods for recovery from illness.
culturalNote: Supu ya mfupa is one of Kenya's most beloved comfort foods and has a legendary status as a restorative meal. At Kenyan butcheries, a cup of hot bone soup is as much a part of the experience as the meat itself — warming, nourishing, and deeply satisfying.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan supu — the butchery version with minimal spice.
Spiced supu — with extra ginger and black pepper.
Goat bone soup — using goat bones for a more intense flavour.
Vegetable-rich supu — with added greens and extra vegetables.
